Tooltip_craft_saltingTubDesc: Presses up to 50 weight of salt-packed fish under a weighted board for 1 to 2 days, longer for bigger fish. Nothing more goes in until the cured fish is taken out.
Tooltip_craft_dryingFrameDesc: Hangs up to 8 stacks of fish, up to 2.5 weight each, in the open air for 12 to 30 days. Salt Cured fish dries fastest in warm, dry weather. Gutted fish needs a cold season, or it spoils. Rain stops the drying.
Tooltip_craft_dryingBeamMediumDesc: Hangs up to 4 stacks of fish, up to 15 weight each, on hooks. Dries like a Fish Drying Frame, for fish too big to hang on one. Open air or under an open roof, not in a room.
Tooltip_craft_dryingBeamLargeDesc: Hangs up to 2 stacks of fish, up to 50 weight each, on hooks. Dries like a Fish Drying Frame, for the biggest fish. Open air or under an open roof, not in a room.
Tooltip_craft_hangFishToDry: Salt drying, for Salt Cured fish. Works in any season, fastest in warm, dry air, best in the shade. Keeps for months.
Tooltip_craft_hangFishToColdDry: Cold drying, for gutted fish and halves. Needs a cold season, out of a room, or the fish rots. Keeps for a year or more.
Tooltip_TraditionalPreservationFishMeat_: Takes 4 salt for each started half weight of the packed fish, about a seventh of its weight. Carry the salt yourself: a shaker holds 10, a Bag of Salt 50. A fish over 4.5 weight is too thick to salt whole: gut and split it first.
Cure it in a Salting Tub before it spoils.
Cured, but not yet preserved. Rinse off the salt if you like (right-click), then hang it on a Fish Drying Frame.
Hang it on a Fish Drying Frame in a cold season, or cook it. Split it if it's too heavy to hang.
Hang it on a Fish Drying Frame in a cold season, or cook it.
Keeps for a year or more. Too hard to eat: rehydrate it in water first.
Keeps for a year or more. Too hard to eat: rehydrate it in water first. Maturing: 0 percent. Ripe stockfish cheers you up once rehydrated.
Keeps for a year or more. Too hard to eat: rehydrate it in water first. Maturing: 10 percent. Ripe stockfish cheers you up once rehydrated.
Keeps for a year or more. Too hard to eat: rehydrate it in water first. Maturing: 20 percent. Ripe stockfish cheers you up once rehydrated.
Keeps for a year or more. Too hard to eat: rehydrate it in water first. Maturing: 30 percent. Ripe stockfish cheers you up once rehydrated.
Keeps for a year or more. Too hard to eat: rehydrate it in water first. Maturing: 40 percent. Ripe stockfish cheers you up once rehydrated.
Keeps for a year or more. Too hard to eat: rehydrate it in water first. Maturing: 50 percent. Ripe stockfish cheers you up once rehydrated.
Keeps for a year or more. Too hard to eat: rehydrate it in water first. Maturing: 60 percent. Ripe stockfish cheers you up once rehydrated.
Keeps for a year or more. Too hard to eat: rehydrate it in water first. Maturing: 70 percent. Ripe stockfish cheers you up once rehydrated.
Keeps for a year or more. Too hard to eat: rehydrate it in water first. Maturing: 80 percent. Ripe stockfish cheers you up once rehydrated.
Keeps for a year or more. Too hard to eat: rehydrate it in water first. Maturing: 90 percent. Ripe stockfish cheers you up once rehydrated.
Keeps for months. Very salty: rehydrate it in water before cooking.
Raw, it will make you sick. Cook it, or add it to a soup or stew. It can't be dried. It also makes chum.
Fish head stock, ready to take up to 6 stew ingredients and your seasonings. It starts out as tasty as a plain stew. Cook it before eating.
Tooltip_craft_rinseSaltedFish: Optional. Soaks the excess salt off Salt Cured fish or meat before hanging, as on the Volga and in the charqueadas. It comes out less salty (less thirst; the fish loses its sour note) but keeps a tenth less long. Near a sink, bathtub, barrel or well, right-click it for Rinse at Sink.
Tooltip_TraditionalPreservationFishMeat_: Rinses %1 pieces with %2 L of clean water from the sink, bathtub, barrel or well close by. It comes out less salty but keeps a tenth less long.
Tooltip_craft_stockfishPalletDesc: Where stockfish ripens, stacked as in the old warehouses. Cold Dried fish on it ripens twice as fast in a loft (a room upstairs) and half as fast again in a ground-floor room; covered, outdoors or in a damp basement, no faster than a shelf. Holds 20 weight.
Tooltip_TraditionalPreservationFishMeat_: Stockfish tied up as it was shipped from the Lofoten. Holds 10 weight of stockfish and nothing else; the fish ripen inside, on a pallet too.
Ties %1 stockfish (%2 weight) into a bale with %3. A bale holds 10 weight; the rest stay out.
Needs Twine or a Rope.
The fish go into your inventory and you get back the %1.
Raw fat from a butchered pig. Put two in a pot and cook it on any stove or fire, pour off the Melted Lard, then strain it. A Hearth's copper melts many pieces at once.
Raw fat from butchered cattle or sheep. Put two in a pot and cook it on any stove or fire, pour off the Melted Tallow, then strain it. A Hearth's copper melts many pieces at once.
Rendered beef or mutton fat. Bakes and seasons like Lard.
The crisp bits left in the pot after rendering fat.
Cook it on any stove or fire. Once it is cooked, pour off the melted fat and strain it. Burnt fat is only good for scraping out.

Beef, Steak, Mutton Chop or Venison, as it is. Takes 4 salt for each started half weight, about a seventh of its weight, as charque. Carry the salt yourself. Pork is not sun dried: its fat goes rancid.
Salted, not yet cured. Cure it in a Salting Tub, one to two days by the heaviest cut.
Cured, but still damp: it keeps a week or two. Cook it, or rinse off the salt if you like (right-click) and hang it on a drying frame to dry in the sun as Charque.
Tooltip_craft_hangMeatToDry: Salt drying, for Salt Cured meat: charque. Best in hot sun and a breeze, about 5 days in summer; slow in spring and autumn, nearly stops in winter. Rain on an open frame takes some of it back. Keeps for months.
Tooltip_TraditionalPreservationFishMeat_: Keeps for months. Salty and as hard as leather: rehydrate it in water before cooking.
Desalted and soft again. Still a little salty. Cook it soon: it spoils like fresh meat.

Beef, mutton, venison or pork cooked slowly in Lard or Tallow with salt, as kavurma and confit are made. Add up to four cuts: a block of fat covers four. Cook it on any stove or fire, then pack it into a clay jar or pot.
Cook it on any stove or fire for about two hours, then pack it into a Clay Jar, Glazed Clay Jar or Clay Pot. Add more meat before it cooks, up to four cuts. Burnt, it is only good for scraping out.

Cooked meat sealed under its fat, a portion a cut. Keeps about 120 days in a fridge or the cold, 60 in a basement; a pantry follows the season, down to 14 days in summer. The first portion taken lets the air in: a third of its time goes. The jar comes back when it is eaten out.
Tooltip_craft_smokehouseChamberDesc: A plank smokehouse two tiles long under one roof slope, its door on the high end. Hangs up to 6 stacks of salt fish or Salt Cured meat, up to 15 weight each. With no fire it dries like a frame in a room: still air, no rain. No cold drying: gutted fish needs open air. Open air or under an open roof, not in a room.
Tooltip_TraditionalPreservationFishMeat_: Cooked through in the smokehouse and ready to eat. Still moist: it keeps a week or two.
